title: Base rates and description: the lawyer-engineer problem and Robert

blocks.text: A **base rate** is how common each category is in the population. The **representativeness heuristic** judges whether something belongs to a category by how well it resembles that category, and **base-rate neglect** is when that resemblance pushes the base rate out of the judgment. It is hard because a vivid description feels like real evidence, while a base rate is just a dry number.
children: Use the numbers first, then adjust for the description.

blocks.text: In the **lawyer-engineer problem**, a group has **70 lawyers and 30 engineers**. With no description, the chance of an engineer is 30 out of 100, and people get this right. When Jack is described as conservative, careful, ambitious and fond of home carpentry, sailing and math puzzles, people call him an engineer and disregard the 70/30 split.
children: People use base rates when nothing else is available and ignore them once a description appears.

blocks.text: **Robert** wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, so many people say he is a librarian rather than a farmer. But America has about **2.2 million farms** and only **120,000 libraries**, so the base rate favors farmer.

title: The conjunction rule and the Linda problem

blocks.text: The **conjunction rule** says that two events together cannot be more probable than either event alone. Every case that satisfies both conditions also satisfies each one. It is hard because a more detailed story feels more likely, even though each added detail narrows the possibilities.
children: Adding a condition can only shrink the set.

blocks.text: In the **Linda problem**, Linda is single, outspoken, bright, a philosophy major, and concerned with discrimination and social justice. About **82%** choose that she is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement over bank teller alone.
children: The extra detail makes the story fit her, so people pick it.

blocks.text: Feminist bank tellers are a **subset** of bank tellers, so being in the smaller set automatically puts her in the larger one. The error is choosing the better-fitting story over the nested-set relationship, which is a **representativeness** effect.

title: Sample size and probability: the hospital problem and the jellybean problem

blocks.text: Both problems show that people attend to what is easy to see and skip the quantity that matters. In the **hospital problem**, a larger hospital has about **45 births a day** and a smaller one about **15**, and about half of babies are boys. The question is which hospital has more days with over 60% boys. The answer is the **smaller hospital**, because small samples vary more, but **56%** said about the same.
children: Small samples swing more, so extreme proportions are more common in them.

blocks.text: The **law of large numbers** says that as more individuals are randomly drawn, the group becomes more representative of the population. People often expect small samples to be representative too. A common slip is choosing the larger hospital, which confuses the total number of boys with how often an extreme proportion occurs.

In the **jellybean problem**, participants earned a dollar for each red bean drawn and chose between **1 red out of 10** (10%) and **7 red out of 100** (7%). Most chose the 7-out-of-100 bowl, because more red beans looks like more chances. A larger count of favorable items draws attention away from the total number of draws.

title: Sacred values: taboo and tragic tradeoffs, moral absolutists, and Ginges and Dehghani

blocks.text: The Sacred Value Protection Model of **Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, and Lerner (2000)** holds that people want to protect what they hold sacred, and that sacred values are kept separate from secular values. A **taboo tradeoff** sets a sacred value against a secular benefit and provokes moral outrage. A **tragic tradeoff** sets two sacred values against each other, and people are less outraged by it.
children: The key confusion is that tragic means two sacred values, and taboo means sacred versus secular.

blocks.text: In the Johnny scenarios, the taboo tradeoff produced much greater outrage when Johnny was not saved than when he was. In the tragic tradeoff, outrage was similar either way. So the decision's effect depends on the type of value conflict, an **interaction**.

**Moral absolutists** treat an issue as sacred and reject compromise regardless of benefit. In **Ginges, Atran, Medin, and Shikaki (2007)**, adding money to a deal increased absolutists' anger, disgust and support for violence, while it reduced these in non-absolutists. Symbolic recognition and an apology helped instead.
children: Money can backfire on sacred issues, and symbolic reciprocity can help.

blocks.text: **Dehghani, Atran, and colleagues (2010)** and **Dehghani, Iliev, and colleagues (2009)** found the same pattern with Iran's nuclear program. For sacred-value participants in the energy condition, approval was lower with 40 billion dollars or with sanctions than with the basic deal, and anger was highest with funds.

title: Confirmation bias and myside bias (2, 4, 6 and Lord and colleagues, 1979)

blocks.text: **Confirmation bias** is the tendency to seek information that fits a hypothesis and overlook information that argues against it. **Myside bias** is one form of it, in which evidence is generated, evaluated and tested in ways that favor one's own opinions and attitudes. It is hard to notice because the evidence feels fair from the inside.
children: Both biases favor what already agrees with you.

blocks.text: **Lord and colleagues (1979)** had people who favored capital punishment and people who opposed it read the same article. Each side interpreted it as favorable to its own position and disregarded the rest. The difference lay in the readers, not the article.

In the **2, 4, 6 task**, participants get 2, 4, 6 as an example of a hidden rule, write their own sets of three numbers, and receive feedback only on whether each fits. The most common hypothesis is **increasing intervals of two**, and testing only sequences that fit it gives repeated yes feedback. The actual rule is **any three numbers in increasing order**, so only trying to disconfirm the hypothesis would reveal that the belief is too narrow.
